newsitem.title: USA: AWAY ON BUSINESS-Crime on the road.
newsitem.headline: AWAY ON BUSINESS-Crime on the road.

text.p: Business travelers trying to make their way through strange surroundings often become prime targets for crime.
Airports, rental cars, hotel corridors and unfamiliar neighbourhoods have all become traps at one time or another for unwary visitors.
Some situations are avoidable. But a book by a retired police officer has some pertinent advice for people who may find themselves victims despite precautions.
Sanford Strong's newly published "Strong on Defence" (Pocket Books, $14 paperback) offers a wide range of advice on coping with crime hazards in various situations.
Some of his advice that is pertinent for travelers:

-- Intersections and parking lots are the most common stalking grounds for car hijackers, who usually operate in pairs and approach the car on foot from either side. Part of Strong's advice where intersections are concerned is to hit the gas, with care, even if the light is red, assuming you're at the head of the line.

-- Intentional bumping or sideswiping a car in traffic, but making it look like an accident, is often a ruse designed for car theft, robbery or worse. Strong suggests the driver stay in his or her car, if necessary telling the other driver to follow along to a well-lit safer place to exchange information. The biggest hazard, he says, is getting out of the car.

-- About half of the people who use a pepper-type chemical spray to ward off an attacker wind up having it knocked from their hands. If that happens, Strong suggests, try to escape rather than trying to get the spray back. He's also sceptical about how useful noisemakers are in a society where people often ignore loud noises and other alarms.
-- Reacting immediately is crucial. In an armed robbery Strong suggests you give up everythng you have and then run away. The longer a confrontation lasts, the worse if gets for the victim, he says.

The travel industry in the last few years has made safety strides. Rental cars are not as easily identifiable on the road by tags or labels, and automatic tracking-mapping devices in some cars can help lost drivers.
Hotels increasingly use key cards, considered more secure than old-style keys, and front desks usually write down a room number for the guest rather than announcing it so that onlookers may hear.
Rooms without an outdoor access are also a safer bet, experts say.
In addition to his specific tips, Strong -- a former San Diego police officer -- advises readers that they need to develop a "survival" mind-set to cope with crime.
